title: Rights groups urge Dhaka to help Ukraine probe trafficking of Bangladeshis into Russian army
excerpt: Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds asked Bangladesh to cooperate with a Ukrainian trafficking investigation. They have documented at least 104 Bangladeshis recruited, with at least 34 reported killed.
content:
Two rights groups, Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds, on Tuesday (24 November) urged Bangladesh to cooperate with a Ukrainian criminal investigation into the trafficking of foreign nationals, including Bangladeshis, into the Russian armed forces, The Daily Star reported. They also asked that the probe examine the role of recruitment agencies and officials in the workers' home countries.

Ukraine's Office of the Prosecutor General announced on 6 November that it had opened criminal proceedings under Part 2 of Article 149 of its Criminal Code, which covers human trafficking, the paper reported. Acting Prosecutor General Anton Kovalskyi said investigators would examine whether representatives of Russian state institutions were involved in recruiting, transporting and transferring foreign nationals for exploitation in the war.

A joint investigation by the two groups found that at least 104 Bangladeshis had been recruited into the Russian military as of February this year, and at least 34 had reportedly been killed. On 26 October, the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine concluded that Russian authorities had trafficked people from 29 countries, including Bangladesh, into the armed forces through deception and coercion, The Daily Star reported.

"People from countries around the world, including Bangladesh, have been deceived, coerced, and exploited by recruitment networks that profit from sending them into Russia's illegal war against Ukraine," said John Quinley, a director at Fortify Rights. Maria Tomak of Truth Hounds said the probe would need full cooperation from the countries concerned, many of which have no agreements or mechanisms for working with Ukrainian prosecutors. The groups urged Ukraine and Bangladesh to screen prisoners of war for signs of trafficking, and asked Dhaka to share material with Ukrainian investigators.

The figures and allegations come from the rights groups and the UN commission as reported by The Daily Star. Devlens has not seen the groups' statement, and the report did not include a response from the Bangladesh government.

Why it matters

The cases show how labour migration channels can be used to deceive workers into combat. Families of those killed or missing need help with information, repatriation and compensation. Migrant-rights NGOs, legal aid groups and anti-trafficking networks have a direct role in identifying victims, supporting families and pressing for action against recruiters in Bangladesh.

What to watch

Whether the foreign and home ministries respond to the call to cooperate, whether any Bangladeshi recruitment agencies face investigation, and whether Bangladeshi prisoners of war in Ukraine are screened and returned home.

Sources
